To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) job demands and job strain are associated with sleep quality and fatigue, and that these associations are stable across time; and (2) changes in job strain are associated, in the expected direction, with changes in sleep quality and fatigue.

(i) job demands and job controls are associated with sleep quality and fatigue, and (ii) cumulative exposure to a non‐high strain work environment is associated with a better sleep quality and lower levels of fatigue.

the effects of work characteristics on sleep quality and the development of fatigue.

the strain hypothesis of the Demand–Control model is supported by our results, and that cumulative exposure to high‐strain work environments is related to elevated levels of sleep quality and sleep‐related complaints.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
job strain is related to poor sleep quality and fatigue, and that the effects of job strain are cumulative and persistent.

The main takeaway from our work is that
sleep quality and fatigue are not only related to current job demands and job resources, but are also related to past job demands and job controls.
the Demand–Control model is a valid and useful framework for understanding and predicting sleep‐related problems at work.
job control is a key factor in the development of sleep‐related problems and fatigue, and that a low‐strain job is associated with better sleep quality.
